name: Aaron Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and also what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a maintenance crew for Ridgeline Power, the regional company, out of the depot on Quarry Road in Pine Ridge. It's hill country, all pine forest, so most of my work is trees. A branch comes down on a line, a whole tree goes over in the wind, and we go cut it clear and put the line back up. I like being outdoors and I like a job that's finished when it's finished. The fire season wears me out, the shutoffs, the heat, people shouting at you because their freezer's warm.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When it's hot and windy, the company cuts power to whole valleys so a line can't spark a forest fire. Makes sense, but we're the ones people see. Then we have to patrol every metre of line before we turn it back on, and that's a long day in a hot truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Can't say I'd be sorry. I don't use it and never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it short, something like, "Well, there you go." I'm not one for posting things. At the depot I'd probably say the company should stop spending money on computer stuff and buy us a new chipper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a relief. I've got about four years left, I'd like to go at sixty-two, and I don't want to learn a new system in my last stretch. I still have the old flip phone, and Grace teases me about it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes, really. I keep turning up, keep doing the work. We've only got about two months of savings after Grace's salon had a bad couple of years, so I'd keep chipping away at that, maybe fifty a week more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the chipper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ours is from 2009 and it jams on anything thicker than my arm. Last month it jammed three times on one job up on Cedar Hill. A new one would save us more time than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grace's salon had a bad couple of years. Is it doing better now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, not good. She's got two chairs and one of them's empty most days since Sandra left. It pays for itself, but it doesn't pay us much.

S0.say: I'd keep it short, something like "well, there you go", because I don't post things. At the depot I'd say the company should buy us a new chipper instead of computer stuff.
S0.think: It's a relief, because I want to retire at sixty-two in about four years without learning a new system. I still use a flip phone and don't plan to change.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and adds about fifty a week to savings that sit at roughly two months of expenses. Asks for a new wood chipper rather than new software.
S0.feel: Calm, like any ordinary working day.
S0.quote: Ours is from 2009 and it jams on anything thicker than my arm.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is plain-spoken and low-key, and his idea of useful technology is a chipper that doesn't jam. His savings are at the thin end of moderate because of his wife's struggling salon. He wants his last four years to be predictable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Changes in many jobs. Hmm. That's the office mostly, I'd guess. But it always comes down to the trucks in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it will help and some won't, let's see. I'm not one to get worked up before something happens. If somebody asked me online, which they wouldn't, I'd say the company should keep it sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry they'll make me use a tablet for everything. They tried that two years ago with a work app and I kept forgetting to log my jobs, and my supervisor, Kevin, had words. I don't think a computer takes my job, but it could make my last years a misery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what they bring in, and only learn it if I have to. If it's a tablet thing, I'd ask Kevin to pair me with someone younger on the crew who can do the logging. I'd keep saving the fifty a week and not spend on anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a squeak in the truck that you know will get worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Kevin actually say when you forgot to log your jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He said, "Aaron, if it's not in the app, it didn't happen." I said the line's back on, that's how you know it happened. We laugh about it now, but he wasn't laughing then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your family whose job you'd worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wen, my daughter, is an accountant. She says half her work could be done by a computer already. She's clever, she'll land on her feet, but I'd worry.

S1.say: I'd say some of it will help and some won't, so let's see. The company should keep it sensible.
S1.think: I don't think AI takes my job, but I worry they'll make me use a tablet for everything and make my last years a misery. My daughter's accounting job worries me more.
S1.do: Waits to see what tools arrive and learns them only if required, asking to pair with a younger colleague for logging. Keeps saving about fifty a week and avoids big purchases.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a small worry he expects to grow.
S1.quote: He said, "Aaron, if it's not in the app, it didn't happen." I said the line's back on, that's how you know it happened.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron's fear here is not losing his job but being made to feel slow in his last years. He avoids opinions until things happen, which fits his middle-ground outlook. His daughter's exposure as an accountant comes up unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots doing line work by 2028. I'd be sixty. Two years before I meant to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say less than most people. Something like, "We'll see what the company does." But inside I'd be churning, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd frighten me. Two months of savings, Grace's salon barely ticking over, and if robots can cut hair too, there goes that. The company's owned by some big fund somewhere, and if robots are cheaper, they'll use robots, that's just how it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra things straight away, the fishing trip in spring, the new boots I've been eyeing. I'd ask around the smaller utilities nearby, Valley Electric in Eastford, because a small outfit might be slower to buy robots. And I'd sit down with Danny, my son, to see if we could lean on each other if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not sleep well, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to Danny about leaning on each other. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a firefighter, so maybe his job's safer, I don't know. If it came to it, maybe we'd rent our house and move into his downstairs flat. I'd hate it, but I'd do it before I'd lose the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't blame the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If you could run a crew without paying four people, you would too. I'd blame whoever let it happen so fast without a plan for people like me, but I couldn't tell you who that is.

S2.say: I'd say less than most people, something like "we'll see what the company does". Inside I'd be churning.
S2.think: It would frighten me, with two months of savings and my wife's salon barely ticking over. The company would use robots if they're cheaper, that's just how it is.
S2.do: Cuts extras straight away, including a spring fishing trip and new boots, and asks about jobs at a smaller nearby utility that might be slower to buy robots. Talks with his son about relying on each other, including possibly moving into his son's flat.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and he expects to lose sleep.
S2.quote: I'd hate it, but I'd do it before I'd lose the house.
S2.fieldNote: There's a big gap between Aaron's quiet public line and his private fear. He doesn't blame the company, seeing cost-cutting as natural, and can't name who should have stopped it. His fallback is family, not the state, and he has thought about it in concrete terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. I'd be sixty-three. So, a year after I planned to go. Closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and there's no point fighting it, we'd better get ready. At the depot I'd say let's talk to the company about how they phase it in. I'd probably not say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I'd just about dodged it. If I can make it to sixty-two, I'm out before it lands. Like I said with the two-year one, the real problem is Grace's salon and our small savings, not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and try to bump savings to a hundred a week instead of fifty. Grace and I would talk about selling the salon in the next few years while it's still worth something. I wouldn't learn any robot stuff, that's for the young ones, I'd just keep my head down to sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the two-year one, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say about selling the salon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say no, then she'd think about it for a week, then she'd say maybe. She's had it twenty years. It's her place, more than a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Would five years of warning tempt you to learn anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If they made me do a course, I'd do it. But I'm not going out looking for one, I'm too old to be the new guy.

S3.say: I'd say it's coming and there's no point fighting it, so we'd better get ready. At the depot I'd suggest talking to the company about how they phase it in.
S3.think: If I make it to sixty-two I'm out before it lands, so I'd feel like I'd just dodged it. The real problem is my wife's salon and our small savings.
S3.do: Keeps working toward retirement at sixty-two and tries to raise savings to a hundred a week. Discusses selling his wife's salon within a few years while it still has value, but avoids learning anything robot-related.
S3.feel: Anxious, though less than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: If they made me do a course, I'd do it. But I'm not going out looking for one, I'm too old to be the new guy.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Aaron's own job clears the landing, so his worry moves to household money and his wife's salon. He would accept change if forced but won't seek it out. The idea of selling the salon is clearly hard for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be long gone. Sixty-eight, sitting on the porch, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so people should plan. I'd tell the young lads on the crew to think about it now. I wouldn't make a big speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think it's not my problem by then, which sounds cold. But my kids would be in their forties, so it is my problem in a way. Wen would be the one I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing and retire at sixty-two. Keep saving what we can. Maybe tell Wen over Sunday dinner to look at what an accountant does when the computer does the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A small worry for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Wen would say over Sunday dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, "Dad, I've thought about it more than you have." And she'd be right. Then she'd change the subject to my flip phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if robots ended up doing your job after you'd gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The early mornings after a storm, when the forest smells of cut pine and the whole crew's working together. Nobody talks much, we just know what to do. I don't know if a robot will get that.

S4.say: I'd say there's plenty of time, so people should plan. I'd tell the young lads on the crew to think about it now without making a big speech.
S4.think: It's not my problem by then, which sounds cold, but my kids would be in their forties. My daughter's accounting work is the one I'd worry about.
S4.do: Keeps working exactly as he is and retires at sixty-two as planned, saving what he can. Raises the subject with his daughter over Sunday dinner.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a small worry for his children.
S4.quote: The early mornings after a storm, when the forest smells of cut pine and the whole crew's working together.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts Aaron safely past retirement, and he admits that makes him care less, then corrects himself for his kids' sake. His fondest memory is of crew teamwork after storms. He remains the same quiet, unshowy man throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It catches me before sixty-two, with not much put by, and it'd hit Grace too. What would help is the company letting older workers go early with their full retirement money, and maybe somebody explaining what we'd be entitled to, in plain words.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees. Robots might put up lines, but the forest doesn't care about robots. Somebody's still got to read which pine is going to fall next winter, and that takes years of looking.

headlineQuote: Robots might put up lines, but the forest doesn't care about robots.
portrait: Aaron Zhang is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker on a maintenance crew for Ridgeline Power in forested hill country, where most of his work is clearing fallen trees from lines. He uses a flip phone, has never used AI and wants to retire quietly at sixty-two. He is relieved by the hype picture and mildly uneasy about being forced onto tablets in the slow one. AGI by 2028 alarms him because his savings are thin and his wife's hair salon is struggling, and his fallback would be family, not the government. With five or ten years he expects to just get out in time, though he worries about his daughter's accounting job.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would catch him before sixty-two with little saved and could hit his wife's salon at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Early exit with full retirement money for older workers, and someone explaining what they'd be entitled to in plain words.
